On the orders of the day:
Mr. ECCLES J. GOTT (South Essex): On a question of privilege, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) as reported in Hansard at page 3275 had this to say on the orders of the day:
Hon. Peter Heenan (Kenora-Rainy River): Mr. Speaker, during my absence from the house on April 24 the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) made a statement which will be found on page 2513 of Hansard. In referring to myself he said:
In the month of March of that year-
That is, 1930-
-he drew $520 sessional indemnity.
I said $620, not $520. He continued:
I have waited for nearly three weeks to try to catch the hon. member in his seat, but I have not been successful. I had hoped to make a correction while the hon. member was present, but I do not think the matter should go any further. I just want to say that that statement is not true.
I have no desire to do an injustice to any hon. member. If that statement is not true, I wish the hon. member had given the correct figures, because his total personal expenses for 1929, exclusive of his sessional indemnity and ministerial salary, were $9,291. His total personal expenses from 1926 to the end of his term in office were $16,691.

The house resumed from Wednesday, May 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 4, respecting the Bureau for Translations -Mr. Cahan-Mr. Bury in the chair.
On section 3-Bureau for translations.

When the committee rose on Wednesday afternoon I was discussing clause 3 of the bill. I wish to direct some further remarks in connection with it in addition to those I have already laid before the committee. As I want to be quite correct in the statements I shall make, and as I intend to offer some suggestions in an attempt to better conditions in the printing bureau in regard to the translation of debates, I shall speak somewhat closely to the notes that I have made. It has not been my practice to read my speeches but I consider this question so important that any suggestions or criticisms I may make should be along definite lines, distinctly understood, and having a basis of correctness.
With that object in view I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that when this bill was up for second reading I stated that the minister could solve the difficulties he had encountered without the introduction of a bill of this kind. At that time I made my suggestions, suggestions which I considered constructive. Those suggestions are to be found in the speech I delivered on March 6 as reported in Hansard at pages 1242-3. I shall read those suggestions again, or rather repeat them. I said it was not fair to criticize a measure unless one was prepared to submit something constructive, and I suggested the following:
Let me, sir, offer some suggestions. First, have it arranged that each department shall have departmental reports ready before the fall of the year and handed to the translators before the English text of the report is printed. At present what do we find? Departmental reports in English are handed to the translators in many cases only after the English edition has come from the printing bureau. This suggests one way of avoiding the tardiness that has worked itself into the printing of the reports. Matters should be so arranged that these reports shall be given to the French translators as soon as the English version is complete, or, better still, as twenty, thirty or forty pages of the copy are completed and certified by the proper authorities, those pages should be handed over to the French translators. It would then be found that the French version would be ready to go to the printer within two or three days after the English version is ready.
Then I went further and said:
It has become an almost universal practice among ministers of the crown-I am not going to include myself in this category; for when I was in the government these reports were ready in time-to delay sending to the printers until the fall of the year the reports for the year ending the previous March 31st. If the minister would issue an order that these reports must be ready soon after parliament prorogued, say the last part of July or the
Translations Bureau

early part of August, there would be no further cause for complaints about tardiness in the printing of those reports.
Further on I made a third suggestion: Do not pass documents to persons outside the service for translation, and fourth: do not allow young bilingual clerks and typists to handle the translation of any documents.
Then fifth:
With reference to the debates of the commons, see that a typewritten copy of the English transcript is handed to the Commons staff of translators just as soon as the English reporters can furnish it, and have the French translators begin translating when they receive that typewritten copy. Instead of doing that, what happens?
And then I go on to explain what happens.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I find that an order in council was passed, I think on May 21st, and laid on the table here last Wednesday. When I was speaking on Wednesday I did not know that that order in council referred to this matter, I learned it the next day in reading the press. Reading that order in council carefully I find that two or three of the most important suggestions made by me on that occasion are included in the document. I am going to read the order in council. It is not necessary to encumber Hansard with the whole of it but, I shall take that part that refers to the point I wish to make. After certain vhereases it says:
That in order to maintain the efficient operation of the printing bureau and to reduce its costs to a satisfactory basis, it is necessary to insure that the supply of printer's copy for printing all departmental reports and' documents shall be balanced uniformly throughout the fiscal year;
That, as the printing bureau is subject to extraordinary demands during the session of parliament for printing and binding the debates and proceedings of the Senate and House of Commons, it is essential for the economic operation of the printing bureau that the printer's copy of all departmental reports to parliament, usually known as "blue books," should be made available to the king's printer, in both English and French, as early as possible after the close of each fiscal year;
That the Secretary of State is reliably informed that the federal government of the United^ States peremptorily insist that the printer's copy for all reports of the several departments of that government shall be available for the printer within three months after the close of their fiscal year; and
That the adoption and strict enforcement of a similar regulation by the government would provide continuous work for the printing bureau uniformly from month to month throughout the fiscal year, and thereby afford constant and continuous employment for the employees of the printing bureau, curtail the excessive cost of overtime night work during the session of parliament, considerably reduce the general expenses of operation of the 
printing bureau, and' enable this department of government to provide an adequate and more satisfactory service at considerably less expense;
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered that it shall be the express duty of the deputy heads of all departments of government to insist that the printer's copy of all departmental reports, complete in revised typewritten form, in either the English or the French language, shall be delivered to the king's printer on or before the first day of July in each and every year;
Now, Mr. Chairman, right here I shall-
The hon. gentleman has spoken for forty minutes.

No, Mr. Chairman, I have
spoken little more than five minutes.

I call the
hon. member's attention to the fact that he spoke half an hour on Wednesday.
I ceased then. In committee of the whole I think I can discuss an item more than once.

The hon. gentleman has a right to speak again. The whole question is whether his speech this afternoon is a continuation of his speech on Wednesday. If it is not, then the position is that any other hon. member of the committee to-day could have risen to speak the moment the committee wms called to order. But the hon. member rose as of right to continue his interrupted speech.
Mr. Chairman-

Before the hon. gentleman
continues I wish to state that when he made his suggestions-

I do not think this is in
order; I have the floor.

The question at present is whether the hon. member is correct in his view that the rules of committee permit a speaker whose speech had been interrupted by the rising of the committee from its previous sitting, when he resumes his speech at the next sitting in committee, to consider that he is recommencing another forty minute period.
It is a new speech.

I think
that is a matter which the committee ought to settle.

I am not resuming; on
Wednesday I finished what I had to say then.

Translations Bureau

Rule 58 provides that the standing orders of the house shall be observed by the committee of the whole so far as may be applicable. In my opinion, though I am prepared to hear members of the committee on the point, a member who has spoken in committee one day has no right to resume bis speech in committee the next day, and to consider that he is commencing a new speech.

Will you please give me
the rule and the paragraph?

Rule 58,
paragraph 1, page 157 of Beauchesne:
The standing orders of the house shall be observed in the committees of the whole house so far as may be applicable-

But it continues:
-except the standing orders as to the seconding of motions and limiting the number of times of speaking.

That has
nothing to do with it. We are not limiting the number of times of speaking at all. This is a simple question as to whether a member of the committee has a right, after having spoken for say thirty minutes on the previous day, to take up another forty minutes when the committee resumes the following day.

Then you establish a new
jurisprudence.

I did not adjourn the
debate on Wednesday. If I had adjourned the debate I think the ruling would be quite right.
The answer to that argument, I think, is that it is not necessary to adjourn the debate; the debate adjourns itself at six o'clock.

Rule 58, which you have just invoked, reads:
The standing orders of the house shall be observed in the committees of the whole house so far as may be applicable

It is well understood that there are a number of rules observed in committee that do not prevail when the house is sitting as a house. In the house no hon. member has a right to put a question to another hon. member except by consent. When the committee is sitting the same rules that prevail in the house apply to a certain extent, but while in the house no questions are allowed, in committee of the whole frequent questions may be asked and answered, so this must be taken mutatis mutandis. 'Under those circumstances I submit that the forty minute
rule of the house cannot apply to the sittings of the committee of the whole. It might be said that the moment the hon. member is interrupted in committee of the whole, immediately his forty minutes is completed and then he can begin all over again. I stood up, and the Secretary of State stood up and interrupted the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would not that be the
best way to settle it? He has been interrupted; let him go on.
Speaking to the point of order-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has been withdrawn.
With the consent of the committee the hon. gentleman may continue, but this is a question that ought to be settled.
If the committee has to settle it I should like to speak to the point of order for a moment.
There is no need to debate it now; the hon. member has the consent of the committee to go on.

You have said that the point ought to be decided, and I want it to be decided now. Rule 37 states that no hon. member shall speak for more than forty minutes during the course of any debate. That rule applies in the house but it does not apply when we are in committee of the whole, because rule 58 states that the rules of the house shall be observed in committee except the rule limiting the number of times of speaking. We are not debating now; we are discussing. In the house we debate; here we discuss, and the Minister of Justice understands that difference very well.
I cannot follow the hon. member's argument, but with the consent of the committee the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) may proceed.

Thank you. I was referring to the order in council and the provision contained therein with regard to the printing of departmental reports. I find that this order in council contains my first suggestion in full, and that it also includes suggestions two and five in substance. Suggestions three and four, which referred to giving translations to clerks and sending translations outside are not referred to in the order in council, and I can understand why it was not necessary to do so; those matters can be arranged by the different
Translations Bureau

departments without the authority of an order in council.
The part of the order in council which refers to the method to be adopted in reference to the translation of departmental reports could be applied with equal force to the production and translation of parliamentary debates, both of this chamber and of the Senate. At page 979 of Hansard for February 27 of this year, in giving reasons for the introduction of this bill the Secretary of State said:
-I was informed, as the minister responsible for the administration of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, that the publications of French translations of public documents were frequently so long delayed as to impair, if not to destroy, their usefulness to the government and to the public.
This statement could leave but one impression, that the delay was due to the translators. When I spoke previously I pointed out how and why this delay was caused. I now find that the Secretary of State must have convinced himself that I was right; he must have looked more fully into the matter, if I am to judge from the order in council that I have just read. This order in council now places responsibility for the delay where it properly belongs, on the various departments of the government and not on the translators. The responsibility for this delay now having been placed on the proper shoulders I hope the Secretary of State will not continue to blame the translation staff.
According to the hon. gentleman, however, we have still another evil; that is, the too great cost for changes that have to be made in type after the translation has been handed to the printer. I have gone into this matter already and have attempted to show that this extra expense cannot be attributed to faulty translation in such large measure as the Secretary of State suggests. If there are errors attributable to faulty translation-and no doubt there is some faulty translation-it cannot be helped in the ordinary course of events. Such faulty translation must exist, to some extent, but there is a remedy for it. All the hon. gentleman has to do is add to the present order in council another suggestion I intend to make, and I want the Secretary of State to give very careful consideration to it. All he has to do is to add to the present order in council the provision that instructions be issued to each department to the effect that no translation shall be sent to the printer until such translation has been revised by the person responsible for the correct translation. This

revision is to be done when the translation has been typewritten, and not after it has been put into type. If this is done, the galley proofs will come back to the translation branch of each department, and be returned practically as a clean sheet. Then the government would further avoid the necessity of furnishing to the translators a loose-page proof. The latter, in itself, will save considerable delay as well as considerable extra cost. That is not being done to-day and the system should be changed in order to bring about the procedure which I am now suggesting. All the Secretary of State has to do is to add the instructions to the present order in council, or have placed in the order in council instructions to the effect of those I have just stated.
But there still remains the author's changes. If, after the galley proof has been submitted to him, the author has made no changes in the English version, there will be no changes made in the French translation. But if the author's changes have to be made, then one may definitely know what those changes are, and what the cost has been in making them. The minister could then quite easily distinguish the charges to be made for errors by authors or errors in translation which, evidently, according to the evidence given before the committee of investigation they are not now in a position to do. I claim that they should now be able to do so. I claim, further, that it is at the present time an easy matter to do so. If it is not done and has not been done in the past, it is because the work of the printing bureau has been carried on in a loose manner. Of course, I am not blaming this government any more than any other government for that condition.
I wish further to point out how unfair some of the criticism made by the Secretary of State has been. Before doing so however, let me say that if in the first two or three years in which he was in charge of the department he had obtained the passage of the order in council tabled last Wednesday, he would not be confronted with the worries which now assail him, and under that order in council, which I claim is the keynote to a solution of the difficulty, we would have a system established. I state that under it there could be established a system which, with the additions I have indicated, would give satisfaction to all concerned, and thereby avoid the necessity of introducing this bill.
On May 9, I find that Mr. F. G. Bronskill gave evidence before the civil service committee, and it is indicated in the evidence that he is the accountant of the printing bureau.

Translations Bureau
In answer to a question by Mr. Chevrier touching upon the question of errors in translation he said-
At what page?

I have not the page, but
I copied the evidence exactly as it appears in the official report. Mr. Bronskill's reply was:
Well, I do not know quite why you refer to translation. So far as we are concerned, it is an author's alteration, that is a change in the proof made by the author. The cost of that for the year 1933-34 is given at $58,000.
Then, in reply to some other questions he said, in substance:
It would be very difficult to tell how much of that money is due to translations,-to French corrections or English corrections.
Then he was asked the following question:
And therefore, it is all put together?
-referring to the $58,000-and the reply by the witness was "Yes." Then comes the following question:
Without knowing exactly what amount is due to the corrections of the French groups and the corrections of the English groups?
A. That is correct, sir.
In the face of such answers from the accountant of the printing bureau surely the Secretary of State cannot blame hon. members for casting very grave doubts on his statements made at- various times and places as to the very heavy cost brought about by changes in type due to faulty translations. I feel the Secretary of State must have been led astray by someone in whom he had great faith, because I do not believe that he would wittingly, himself, commit such an error in regard to the cost of translations. Apparently the official merely guessed, and gave the minister the result of such guess work. Now that they have been driven to separate the cost of errors by authors and errors by translators they cannot do so, and the minister has been left to bear the brunt of the criticism. Is it not time that the minister disciplined the printing bureau? He must now know that the-

Mr. Bronskill is not under
my jurisdiction as Secretary of State, as the minister having charge of the printing bureau.
He is the accountant of it.

He is an accountant in the
Department of Finance. I do not know whether he has been there three months or six months.
He is in the printing bureau.
He may be there now, but I do not know how long he has been there, He is not under my supervision.
He is an able man.

Before the committee, as one of his qualifications he stated he was the accountant of the printing bureau. Is it not time that the minister disciplined the staff of the printing bureau-not only Mr. Bronskill but the whole staff? The witness before the committee said he could not distinguish the difference in cost between the corrected French translations and authors' errors. I think it is time that this gentleman was told it is his duty to do that, and that if he does not do it someone else may be obtained who will do it. I would advise the minister to apply his knowledge of organization to the accounting branch as well as to the directing branch of the printing bureau.
I have no control over it,
No control over the printing bureau?
Over the accounting.
I said direction, as well as accounting.
I have no control over the accounting.
But I have added to the word "accounting" the word "directing."
I have it, and I have ex-, ercised it.
It shows the absurdity of centralization.

Following the question of the unfairness which I claim has characterized the criticisms by the Secretary of State on this matter of faulty translations let me come to another point in connection with which I believe he did not do justice to himself or to the matter under consideration. I refer to the evidence given by the Secretary of State before a certain committee. I find Mr. Cahan saying, "I can show you instances of French translation of Senate work that did not come out until a year after the meeting was held." The minister seems to be obsessed by French translations; it seems to be his bete noire. But he does not say a word about delays in printing English versions.
Then an hon. senator took up the cudgels apparently for the translator or for the cost of translation. What do we find? The senator said, "Until this year we did not
Translations Bureau

have much cause for complaint in respect to the French translation of Senate proceedings, but this year the government cut off our money for translation, and we have no translation."
Hear, hear.
In reply to that Mr. Cahan said, "I did not know that."
Hear, hear.

I am surprised to find an astute minister, such as the Secretary of State, giving such a reply. Some discussion then took place as to the difference in cost between having documents printed by the printing bureau and by outside printers, and what do we find? Senator Sharpe said:
Senate translation in French costs for 85 copies $4,519 on the average but that work can be done outside for $2,760.
I want those figures to be noted, and also what follows:
Hon. Mr. Cahan: I have no doubt it could be done for that if clean proofs were handed in. But look at the way the proofs come to us. Here are specimens.
Mr. Sharpe: Surely clean proofs would not be responsible for so much difference in cost.
Senator Sharpe was quite right. Clean proofs could not account for one-quarter of the difference in cost referred to by him.
I will show you the difference in a few moments.

I hope the minister will
bring along a little better evidence than what has so far been produced because he has not yet convinced the members on this side of the house, nor has the committee been convinced I am sure from the evidence already produced before the investigating committee, that there was any necessity for this bill.
Then we have the statement of the bon. the Secretary of State at page 982 of Hansard of February 27 of this year. He said:
Now it was ascertained by one of the committee under the control of the treasury-
I want this to be noted:
-that the setting up in type of these corrections made in the text after it had been set up in type and sent for revision-not all French, but a great deal of it, some of it being in English-over a series of years, in wages in respect of the resetting of that type after it had been first set up in the printer's text, varied in cost from $75,000 to $80,000 a year.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, in the face of that statement I have just quoted we have been unable to ascertain what was the cost of the
[Mr. Veniot.J
corrections of the French text as distinct and separate from the rest. Apparently the committee under the control of the treasury had ascertained that in detail or no such statement could have been made by the Secretary of State. Why has not the report of that committee been brought before the civil service committee of this house so that it would be in possession of the facts? It is no answer to say that the civil service committee had the opportunity of asking for that report. It is no answer to say: You could have examined the witnesses, because the names of the members of that committee 'have been completely hidden from this house. We do not know who the members of it were, or who was. the person who made the report to the governor in council.
The names are on the records of this house.
But that report was never submitted to the civil service committee.
The names of that committee were reported to the house.
They are members of the council, are they not?
They were not.
I do not see their names on the records of this house. I would like to see them.	.
The minister time and again has said that that was a privileged report.
Quite so. The hon. member was asking about the names of the committee.
What is the use of handing out names if you cannot discuss the report of that committee?
He said he could not get the names and I said they were on the records of this house.

I hope the hon. gentleman will produce them. Why is the report of that committee not now before the committee of the whole house for our consideration? Why keep it back from this committee? It should be produced and laid on the table so that this committee would have the opportunity of looking into it and seeing how and when and where the committee based their charges of extra cost against translation and against authors' corrections. We have a right to ask for that, Mr. Chairman, and the minister should produce that report so that we may judge whether this bill is the remedy for all

Translations Bureau
the difficulties that have been specified by him. We should know what the reasons were for the introduction of a bill such as this.
Now I wish to touch upon the work of the printing bureau as done by unilingual and bilingual operators. As I understand it-I may be astray but I think I am correct-when the departmental reports in English are sent to the printer the whole staff of operators, unilingual and bilingual, are put to work upon them, and in that way the English edition can be rapidly got out because the whole staff is working on it. But when the French translation from that English edition is sent to the printing bureau for putting into type the employees who do that work are bilingual employees, only, not unilingual and bilingual as in the case of the English edition, and that is the reason for the accentuated delay in the issuing of the French editions of these reports.
Is the hon. gentleman speaking of bilingual compositors or translators?

I am talking of linotype operators and compositors. I say that the French translation of the English version is handed to the bilingual operators to be set in type and they have to rush that work through notwithstanding that they were able to devote all the time that was required to carry on the unilingual typesetting and linotype operation of the English version.
But, Mr. Chairman, if my proposition is accepted and the two versions are submitted simultaneously in English and in French-by simultaneously I do not mean to say that the English and French versions should be ready at the same time, but the French translation of the English version could be submitted fifteen or twenty pages at a time, and then you would have the operators in the bureau continuously employed and the minister would not be beset by the problems confronting him to-day in trying to keep the whole staff regularly employed. Further, he would be in a position to do away with all this rush work and would be able to have a timely regulation of the work carried on at the printing bureau. That is impossible under the present system. He must change that system in order to do it. The change I suggest would result in a saving to the government and in the work being done efficiently.
I come now to the question of the cost of corrections. I have studied this matter very carefully. I do not wish to repeat what I said on Wednesday and go into this whole 74726-212
question again, but when I was speaking on that day I was not speaking in any boastful way as some hon. members opposite sought to imply. I have the experience which enables me to deal with questions of this kind, especially as to cost, and I think I can direct the minister to a proposition which would enable him to ascertain definitely where the cost lies and how the matter should be treated in the future if he wishes to avoid these extra costs.
First of all I claim that we have a right to know, and if the printing bureau cannot give this information they are not worthy of holding the positions they hold, and as well it would be interesting for this committee to know the definite cost of corrections in faulty French translation which have to be made after setting the copy up in type. We should also be informed as to the exact and definite cost of making authors' corrections in type and putting the material in proper shape in English and in French. Let me direct the attention of the committee to the fact that the law bills submitted to the House of Commons and to the Senate contain more author's corrections in English than in French. There are no corrections in French unless the author of the English text is forced to correct. To correct what? The faulty construction of the bill which he has prepared for the government. The committees of this house are authors because changes are made and bills are brought back to be reprinted. Everything which pertains to these changes must be eliminated from the original bill and the changes correctly inserted. In this way the changes in English are the sole basis of the extra cost of changes which must be made in the French text.
That is far from the case.

That is not far from being so. The only extra cost which can be attributed to the French text is the revision of faulty translation which has been discovered. I admit that there has been some faulty translation but the printing bureau should be in position to distinguish between the cost of faulty translation and the cost of corrections in French due to author's errors and changes made by the committee of the whole house and other committees. I am convinced that the costs of theise changes in legislation and so forth will amount to at least fifty per cent of the $58,000. I challenge the Secretary of State to produce to this committee one account which will disprove the statement I am going to make. I challenge him to produce an itemized and detailed statement of the cost of corrections because of faulty trans-

Translations Bureau

lation. If that is done I know he will find that that which can he properly charged to faulty translation will not amount to ten per cent of the $58,000. I make that statement without fear of contradiction.
The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

At least ten minutes of my time has been used up in the discussion of points of order and so forth. It will take me only about three minutes to complete what I have to say and then I will speak no further on this bill. You will be saving time by allowing me three or four minutes.
I have dealt with the extra cost entailed by authors' corrections and corrections in faulty translation, I have made suggestions which were considered to be sufficiently of a constructive nature to warrant inclusion in the order in council, I have submitted further constructive suggestions to-day which I am sure would be effective if applied, but I have still a further suggestion to make. In view of the strong opposition to this bill as expressed in the house and in the press, in view of the fact that several heads of departments such as the acting Deputy Postmaster General, the assistant director of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the chief of translation of debates have not approved of the changes contemplated, in view of the fact that the order in council which has just been passed will, if put strictly into effect, meet the major difficulties with which the minister is faced, would it not be well for him not to force this bill through but take one year in which to work out the suggestions contained in the order in council? In that time a fair trial could be had and if the suggestions contained in the order in council did not prove effective, then this measure could be put into effect.

Due I suppose to his experience in the printing business, the hon. member has made some suggestions which are more or less valuable. I only regret that he did not use his experience for the benefit of my predecessor in office as then I would not have been overwhelmed with the difficulties which I now face.
The question never arose.

With respect to the suggestions which he made in the house on March 6, 1034, I made the following statement which appears at the top of page 1242 of Hansard:
I fully agree with what the hon. member has said so far.
Why did you not put them into effect?

They have been embodied in an order in council but the provisions of the order in council are inadequate to overcome the difficulties with which I have been confronted. If the hon. gentleman thinks that I have not given attention to the printing bureau then he is very much mistaken.
I did not wish to leave that impression.

The mere cost of printing, binding and lithographic work plus the cost of paper for the year ended March 31, 1930, amounted to $2,482,851.95. For the last year for which accounts have been made, that is the year ended March 31, 1933, these operating costs of the printing bureau amounted to $1,709,494.49. There are several lines of
arguments that may be taken with regard to this bill bub the first point is to see how the translation business is going on at present,
how the translation is done. If the members of the committee will look at the back of report No. 5, page 156, they will see a list of 45 units. In some of those there are no official translators. Is that because no translations are made there? No sir. The reason is obvious-I would ask that the Clerk of the House do not disturb the chairman of the committee while I am addressing the committee, he is mumbling loudly and he disturbs me. There are 45 units. What I was saying when I was disturbed by the mumbling of the Clerk of the House is this, that there is a distinction to be made between translators de facto and the people who are called translators in the estimates. In all departments apparently there is some translation done, but some of it is done by people who are not officially called translators. For instance we have the biological board, which comes under the Minister of Marine, with no translators. Apparently the work is done by the translators of the Marine department. The Canadian pension commission, no translators, but the work is done by the translators of the department. For the Canadian radio broadcasting commission there is no report about translations made. That work is probably done by Mr. Maher who is the bilingual commissioner or Mr. Landry, the bilingual secretary of the board. The chief electoral officer is Mr, Castonguay. There is no translator there; the work is done by Mr. Castonguay who is bilingual and his bilingual staff. In the civil service commission Mr. Potvin is bilingual and he must have some bilingual assistants. Extra work is done outside, and the lack of supervision is due to the fact that t'he translator of the civil service commission was superannuated and has not been replaced. Then the exchequer court is a special case. One of the judges is bilingual and the other is English-speaking, therefore there is no necessity for having an official translator. The work is done by the staff, and the judgments, as you know, Mr. Chairman, because you are a distinguished member of the bar, are printed in the language in which they are given, either French or English. External Affairs, one translator. Farm loan board, no translator. The Department of Finance has no translator except one who is engaged on the railway work; it is curious that a translator who does some work on account of the Department of Railways and Canals does not come under the jurisdiction of my genial friend the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), but of his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). This is wrong

and should be remedied. For the government contracts' supervision committee there is no translator. For the Governor General's secretary's office the translation is done by the staff. Department of Insurance, no translator. International joint commission, apparently no translator. Department of Justice, translations in the official languages are made by Mr. Fontaine, one of the officials of the department, an able bilingual gentleman, and the foreign correspondence is done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Library of parliament is like the exchequer court; one of the librarians is bilingual and they have a bilingual staff, therefore there is no necessity of having translators there. In the national research council the work is done by the staff. The pension appeal court work is done by the Department of Pensions, they have no translator. :In the Department of Public Printing and Stationery the work is done by the staff. The Solicitor General is bilingual, he has a bilingual staff and does not need a special translator. For the supreme court the situation is the same as that in connection with the library and the exchequer court. Mr. Justice Rinfret and Mr. Justice Cannon are bilingual and they have a bilingual staff, therefore there is no necessity for translators. The tariff board has no translators but the work is done by the Post Office Department.
In those 19 units the work is supposed to be done within the staff, there are no translators. In the other units there are some translators. This gives a general summary of the situation. According to the answers which have been sent by every branch there are no translators in the library of parliament, where there are two librarians, one being bilingual, and no translator in the government contracts supervision committee. There are some self-sustaining departments with regard to translation; by that I mean departments which do not send translation outside. One of them is the archives, where excellent work is being done by two translators. Then in the department of the auditor general, who is also bilingual, they have one translator, and the work is done there. For the superintendent of bankruptcy the work is done by the staff, none sent outside. In the Department of Fisheries they have one translator who does the whole work including the annual report. For the Governor General's secretary's office the work is done by the assistant secretary. Indian Affairs has one translator, they do all the work within the department. The Department of Marine have one translator, they do all the work within the department. For the national research council the

work is done by the staff, none sent outside. The Department of National Revenue and customs and excise has three translators, no work sent outside. Public printing translation is done by officers of the department, no work sent outside. The Privy Council have one translator, no work sent outside. Public Works department has three translators, no work sent outside. Soldiers' settlement board work is done by a bilingual member of the staff. Trade and Commerce and bureau of statistics, all work is done in the department, except for a few pages of the blue book last year, but this is an exception. When I asked the Department of the Secretary of State to tell the committee if all the translation was done within the department the answer was, "No information on file respecting translation done by another department and outside the government service." In the patent and copyright office they had also one translator. It means, sir, that in all those branches the work of translation is so organized that all the work is done within the branch.
Let us see which departments have to depend on other departments for the translation of foreign correspondence. From September, 1931, to date the Department of Agriculture sent ninety-two foreign letters to the Department of the Secretary of State. The Department of Labour sent three 'letters during the same period, though the Secretary of State's department say there were six. From the Department of Mines one hundred and eight pages of text were sent to the Department of the Secretary of State, but there is nothing in the report of that department about it. The Department of National Defence sent seven letters, and they sent ten pages outside to be translated. In 1932 the income tax branch had eighteen forms and forty-two pages translated by government translators, and in 1933 they had twenty-two forms and forty-one pages translated by outside translators. It is wrong for the Department of National Defence and for the income tax branch to send their work outside the service; that work is most confidential, and the translation should be done within the service. Occasionally the pension commission sent foreign matter to the translators of the Department of the Secretary of State and the Post Office Department. In 1932-33 the Department of Pensions and National Health sent one hundred and fifteen foreign letters to the Post Office Department.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in addition to what I have already said, we have the departments of agriculture, labour, mines, national defence, pensions and national health and the

Translations Bureau
income tax branch and pension commission having their translation in both languages done within each of these departments, and only a small amount of foreign work is sent outside the service. As a consequence those units are also self-sustaining. Then, with regard to the Department of External Affairs, in the last two years that department sent twenty-4our foreign letters to the Department of the Secretary of State and forty-seven pages to the House of Commons. That is a very small amount. In the Department of the Interior the head translator had to deal with ten thousand items in two years, and he sent two hundred letters and ten articles to the Department of the Secretary of State, though that department gives the amount as fifty-five letters and certificates and four hundred and twelve pages of technical matter. In 1932 that Department sent one hundred and forty-one pages and in 1933 they sent one hundred and thirty-two pages to the blue book branch of House of Commons, in addition to ten or fifteen legal documents to the law branch of the House of Commons. Formerly there were many translators in the Department of the Interior; there was no reason why all should have been dismissed with the exception of only one. In his evidence Mr. Bland said that in this department there would be enough work for two translators, so one man from the blue book branch should be sent to the Department of the Interior to assist the translator already there. That is the first department of all those I have mentioned that is not self-sustaining, and that is so because there are fewer translators engaged in the work. It is very easy to remedy that condition. One must be fair; the translator in that department must be given some assistance.
It seems unfair that some translation work done for the Department of the Interior should be charged to the House of Commons. There is no reason why we should pay for the work done for that department. The estimates of the Department of the Interior show a reduction, but on the other hand there is a proportionate increase in the estimates for the House of Commons. This is absurd; the work should be charged to the department for which the work is done.
Now let us consider the work done by the blue book branch of the House of Commons for the civil service commission. The reports of 1932 and 1933 were translated by that branch. This is wrong. The translator of the civil service commission was superannuated, and the position has not been filled. Mr. Bland told the committee that there would be
enough work to give employment to one translator within the civil service commission, translating the official reports and revising the corrections. Why is that not done? Those publications of the civil service commission, advertisements of vacant positions and so on, should be done very carefully. They go all over the country, and they should be well done. It is necessary that they should be revised, and in addition there is no reason why the civil service commission should send its work to the House of Commons. If some money is to be voted for the civil service commission I have no objection, provided that it is charged to the civil service commission and not to the House of Commons. The audit board should see to that, because it is a discrepancy in accounting. The money should be charged to the department for which it is expended, and I take this opportunity of directing the attention of the government to that point.
Then there is the Department of Finance, whose translation work is done in a very stupid way. Some of it is done by the Post Office Department and some by the blue book branch of the House of Commons. There was a Mr. Lorans who was a translator in the Department of Finance; he died, but the position has not been filled. According to the evidence given by the deputy Minister of Finance, in 1932 there were 246 pages and 925 pieces and in 1933, 348 pages and 1,100 pieces, plus forty references of the tariff board, sent from the Department of Finance and the tariff board to the House of Commons and the Post Office Department for translation. This is absurd; the Minister of Finance should have his own translator, and the work of that department should be done by a man who is familiar with that work.
Then let us take the report of the Post Office Department. According to the deputy minister they have translated 1,300 pieces from the Department of Finance and 900 pages from the tariff board per annum during the last two years. Do you see, sir, the absurdity of refusing to replace the dead translator, and sending some of those translations to the department headed by the Postmaster General and other work to the House of Commons? The Minister of Finance should have the guts to have some estimates for translating services in his own department. It would be possible for a translator to look after tariff board translations and translations for the Department of Finance. The superintendent of insurance also is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance. The farm loan board also comes under his jurisdiction. Do hon.
Translations Bureau

members not think that there would be enough work in these branches I have indicated to employ the services of one translator, and to justify the Minister of Finance bringing forward an estimate for a salary equal to that received by the dead translator who has not been replaced? In that way the work would be done within the department. The work could be done by a translator of the blue book branch who by order in council and according to law could be transferred. Not in 1932, but in 1933 the Department of Immigration sent only ten pages to the blue book branch. Therefore we must conclude that this department is self-sustaining, so far as translation is concerned.
Then there is the board of railway commissioners. In 1931 a report of 131 printed pages was sent to the House of Commons, and in
1932	the house received a report of 72 printed pages from the board. In 1932 the Department of Railways and Canals sent a report of 212 pages to the House of Commons and in
1933	sent a report of 92 pages. While the Minister of Railways formerly had two translators in his department he has now only one.
They never translated blue books. They are translators for correspondence, and that sort of thing, 'but not for blue books.

Even if they did not translate reports, I say it is a bad practice, because the reports of the Department of Railways and Canals should be translated within his department, as the reports and publications of the Department of Finance and other departments are translated within those departments. I should like to see my hon. friend come to the house with a supplementary estimate providing for the salary of one of the translators in the blue book branch, so that that amount might be charged to his department. I should be glad to vote the amount, and in my opinion it would be more proper to have the translator in his own department than to have a messenger going hither and thither from the west block to the house carrying work to be translated outside the department.
May I suggest to the hon. member that if we did that we would have to hire, the year round, a translator to do only one job which would take a matter of two or three weeks, at the most.
Before that there were two translators who seemed to have enough work to do.
They did not; that is why we let one go.
There were two translators on the board of railway commissioners and two translators in the Department of Railways and Canals.
I have nothing to do with the board of railway commissioners. They are an independent body, and with the exception of putting their report before the house I have nothing to do with them.
But at the same time, as to a certain extent they come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways-
No, not at all.

Well, even if they do not come under his jurisdiction, I say that the kind of translation done by the board is about the same kind as is done in the Department of Railways and Canals. I think the minister would admit that. In my view it would be normal to have one translator added to the one now operating in the Department of Railways and Canals in order that that department may have two and in order that the translations may be made by persons who have real knowledge of the railway business and are familiar with railway terms. That work could be done much better, much more quickly and with better results. Anyway, I have submitted my request and if as a result the minister brings an estimate before the house indicating compliance with my suggestion, I shall be very glad.
Fifty pages were sent to the House of Commons blue book branch in 1932 by the Department of Trade and Commerce, statistics branch. That is an exception, because as a rule they do their own work. Only an occasional translation is done for them by the blue book branch. In connection with the Department of Justice, in the year 1932-33 three reports of the superintendent of penitentiaries were sent to the House of Commons. Letters in foreign languages from convicts are sent to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and are not translated in the east block. Most of these departments, with the exception of the Department of Finance, the Department of Railways and Canals and the board of railway commissioners, are self-sustaining so far as translation services are concerned.
The following units are self-sustaining: Agriculture, Archives, Auditor General, Superintendent of Bankruptcy, Fisheries, Governor General's Secretaries, Indian affairs, Marine, National Research Council, National Reve-

Translations Bureau
nue, customs and excise, public printing, Privy Council, Public Works, Soldier Settlement Board, Trade and Commerce, Agriculture, Labour, National Defence, Income Tax, pension commissioners, Pensions and National Health, External Affairs, Immigration, statistics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, with the exception of the superintendent of penitentiaries, the Department of Justice, etc.
The civil service commission is not selfsufficient. The others which are not self-sustaining are the Department of the Interior, where the number of translators has been too much reduced; the Department of Finance, where the dead translator has not been replaced; the Department of Railways and Canals, and the board of railway commissioners, where the number of translators has been reduced.
The hon. member has spoken forty minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at length in this discussion, because I believe I have already stated my views with regard to this bill. To anyone who may express surprise at our opposition may I say, first, that we do not know exactly how the bill would operate. I do not see any ground for such a bill either in Canada or outside of Canada, and I believe the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) would have been much wiser had he given us his reasons for introducing the measure.
I might remind the hon. gentleman that that was settled on the second reading. It is now a matter of the contents of clause 3.
I will come to that.
He has the right to go on.
He has not.
It was granted on Wednesday.
If the committee granted the right to a general discussion on the short title clause, such concession certainly does not apply to every clause of the bill.

Clause 3 provides that there shall be a bureau under the minister to be called the bureau for translations, and it is to that clause I am speaking. I usually do not abuse my right to speak in this house, and I am surprised, Mr. Chairman, that you interrupted me when I was just making a few preliminary remarks on this bill.
As I was saying, I do not see any ground for the centralization of the translation services. Here in Canada if you will look back over the past, you will not find in the record anything in favour of this measure. Look over the rest of the world, more particularly at the experience in Switzerland and Belgium, and you will find that centralization has not produced the effect in those countries that was expected of it, and now they are returning, more particularly in Switzerland, to the system of decentralization.
This bill seems to have been born in the dark like a mushroom, and to my taste it has not even the flavour of a mushroom. When we ask for reasons the minister gets up and speaks, as he. did on two previous occasions, of the printing necessities, as if translation were to be subordinated to printing. That, as we say in French, is "mettre la charrue devant les boeufs,"-to put the cart before the horse; for translation, which after all is a form of writing, and not an easy form, perhaps indeed the most difficult of all, cannot be subordinated to the printing bureau. I do not see why the minister insists upon the necessities of the printing bureau. He went on to give examples. I have always thought a great deal of the fairness of the minister and I was surprised this afternoon when he referred to a very exceptional case where a man who was overworked and had the assistance of some temporary employee without any experience in that particular work turned out to the printing bureau under very difficult ^ conditions a translation which I must admit was not in proper form. But that was very exceptional. It was a case in the Senate, moreover, where we have no jurisdiction, and we have not all the data to deal with it. It does not give us a real picture of the translation services in general, and I am surprised that the minister resorted to that kind of example. When we were pressing him for the author of the translation of the last speech from the throne we were turned down and the minister said that he was shielding someone. I happen to know this man myself. I think very highly of him, and it is not his fault if there were perhaps sixty mistakes in the translation of the speech from the throne. He was perhaps overworked. But it does show one thing; it is an argument against the centralization of translation. How can you expect a man, even a chief translator, to be a master in all kinds of translation? A translator who is working on penitentiary documents will be able to translate such docu-

Translations Bureau

merits very well, and a translator from the Department of Railways can be expected to translate well a report of the Department of Railways, and so on. But the very fact that this speech from the throne is the worst piece of translation that one can witness does not indicate that the translator himself is a poor translator. On the contrary, it indicates that centralization is very unwholesome. Referring again to the speech from the throne, the minister said that he wished to shield the author of this piece of translation, and in order to confute mv hon. friend from Temis-couata and myself, he quoted a letter signed by a pen name. Then in almost the same breath he read another letter, but only in part. Well, Mr. Chairman, when the opposition is asking for information I think we are entitled to get all the information the minister has, and if he had given all the information that was in his possession or had taken the trouble to inform the committee as to the nature and purport of this bill in its working out, perhaps the opposition would not have been so great. But we know nothing whatever about it. We do not know how it will work. We are asked to make the change without being given the facts.
I admit frankly, as I have admitted previously, that a little more coordination is necessary in the different translation offices. So much is that the case that the translators themselves of their own initiative some time ago formed a society called the Technological Institute, where they discuss questions concerning their occupation. That body might be strengthened, or the chief translator in each of the departments might be united in a sort of federation comprising all the departments, with a view to bringing about a further improvement, in translation.
But I resent more than anything else the argument which the minister used and the comparison he made between the translation system and an accounting system. The minister who introduced this bill was unable to have a proper translation made in his own department, and any time that he resorted to the gratuitous services of a friend he never came back with the best piece of work, as has- been demonstrated. The minister now comes and says that he wants to organize the translators in all departments. We do not know if he intends to bring all these translators into one office where one translator will be doing one job and then a few hours afterwards be asked to do another job. I should like to impress upon this committee the impossibility of any man translating the work

of any department unless he is closely related to the activities of that department. New words come up every day and he must be able to follow the technique of the department. In Switzerland instead of looking for mere translators they look for expert scholars and men of great technical ability. These men are part of their department, promotions are open to them and they know just what are the necessities of their department. That is the only way in which there can be good translation. W'e do not know if there is to be a bureau in which all translators will be coordinated or if there is to be just a bureau comprising them all.
There is another point upon which I should like to touch for a few minutes. It has been a long established tradition that the translators of th.e Senate and the House of Commons should be segregated and receive special treatment. They are responsible for their work to the Speakers and to the two houses. Does any hon. member who makes a speech feel it is fair that the translation of that speech should be in the hands of the government? Is it fair that the government should take the responsibility of translating my speech? Is it fair that the translation of my speech should be in the hands of my opponents? The translators of the House of Commons live side by side, so to speak, with the members. They know not only the different idioms used but they know the idiosyncrasies of the different members. If I have' any complaints to make, I make them to the Speaker, and I take full responsibility for the translation of my own speeches. Otherwise I am in the hands of the government. Many hon. members who spoke gave us some hope that a special branch would be established for the parliamentary translators but now we have this bill without the slightest intimation that this is to be done. We should like the minister to be more precise. We should like him to take into consideration the suggestions made from this side of the house and the recommendations made by his colleagues, such as the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau), the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) and others. If he had listened to those suggestions and amended the bill accordingly, he would not be witnessing the strong but sincere opposition we are making to-day.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

Entomology, including investigations and inspections relating to destructive insects and pests, $350,000.

I wonder if the minister has any information regarding the experiment being carried out in the Fraser valley in regard to the health of animals. Two rather interesting orders in council were tabled here the other day, which indicate that $500,000 in the one instance and $1,500,000 in the other have been loaned to the Saskatchewan government for relief and grasshopper control. The Prime Minister said this had been done several weeks ago, and I think the committee is entitled to an explanation. This matter was brought up last Friday, and the recommendation to council may have been prepared on Saturday. At all events it went through by Monday at the latest, according to a statement in the Regina Leader made by Premier Anderson, which says that $500,000 has been loaned for grasshopper control. That is dated Tuesday; the announcement was made last Monday, so the orders in council with respect to this $2,000,000 must have been passed after the discussion last Friday, though the Prime Minister said that considerable amounts had been granted for the same purpose two weeks ago. I have examined or have had examined every order in council back to January, and I have not found any order in council earmarked for grasshopper control; anything that has been done has occurred since the discussion. I think the Prime Minister owes the committee an explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Half a million dollars
had been expended in connection with grasshoppers long before the discussion took place in this house last Friday. The government of Saskatchewan requested that we make them an advance, and they secured their money from the bank, because at the moment there were other provinces in the same position. So when the order in council was prepared and put through part of the money had been obtained from the banks, and we were paying the money when we were in the most convenient position to do so. There has been an additional loan of $750,000 to Saskatchewan since that time. The truth is, that their revenues have been disappointing, while the revenues of some of the other provinces have been larger than was expected.
So far as the grasshopper matter is concerned, as I said the other evening we had arranged to make a loan. It happened that at the very time we were discussing the matter here a telegram was in transit from the west saying that they now had expended the full half million dollars and asking if it would be convenient for us to forward the money, which we did on the following day. The other sums were for general purposes, some of them for our share of relief for which we were obligated under an agreement made last year. We extended the time for works that were partly completed and continued to pay direct relief on the basis of the agreement of last year for the months of April and May. The Minister of Labour advised all the provinces by telegram that we would continue to make relief payments for April and May on the same terms as provided' by the agreements of 1933.
These recent orders in councils are for loans, of course?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, except with respect to relief, where we have the obligation under the agreement. The others are loans, as the hon. gentleman says.

I think the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) must have been sound asleep for the past year or so. Otherwise he would know that we have had a grasshopper plague out in the west and that we have the most complete organization for fighting it that ever existed in the Dominion of Canada. I think this committee should know what is being done. Our farmers have been thoroughly educated during the winter months; winter classes were held all over the province because our agricultural department discovered there were sixteen million acres of land infested with grasshopper eggs. The educational campaign was led by

the entomological department of the university of Saskatchewan, with which is associated the entomological branch of the federal government. We have a very intelligent department out there, notwithstanding my hon. friend from Melville, and all our municipalities were thoroughly organized to fight this plague; they have held mutual councils regularly.
Some people call these pests grasshoppers while some call them locusts. I believe locusts is the biblical term, but I never use that term. If anyone has ever faced this plague, as I have faced it, they would know it is something that must be faced in a very heroic manner and I am very glad that this organization of which I speak has been carried on quietly with the assistance of the Minister of Agriculture. There is no doubt about the assistance that has been given by the federal department, nor is there any doubt about what the agriculture department of the province of Saskatchewan has done and is doing to-day. There is no doubt about what the municipalities are doing, so we need not be afraid that we will not do our part, the hon. member for Melville to the contrary notwithstanding. The hon. gentleman can find all the fault 'he wishes; I do not care. We are going to fight this plague, and we will succeed. The best news I have heard from Saskatchewan in five years was the news that recently, in the country from which I come, copious rains have fallen. The five year drought has been broken, and nothing will do more to destroy these grasshoppers than the rains which have fallen in the last few days. I hope my hon. friend from Melville will rejoice with the rest of us that Saskatchewan is at last coming back.
I have not been closely following .this method of doing business, but I gathered from the Prime Minister that this money had been expended previously. Was that correct?

It has been spent in the preparation campaign? The grasshoppers are just hatching now.

speechtext:

I am not asking the member for Long Lake, because he does not know anything about this matter. I am asking the Prime Minister.
All right, go on.
Last year?

No, this year; it
was in the winter time, preparatory to this spring's work. There were representatives from the dominion department and from the provincial departments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It was agreed to make a united effort against this menace or pest. The United States voted $2,000,000 and undertook to carry on their campaign under federal auspices. Those who have watched the campaign and the effect of preparation for it feel that at a cost of $700,000 in the three prairie provinces the work done under our methods will be more effective or at least as effective as that carried on by the federal government of the United States. That is so, because the fact that they are undertaking the whole responsibility, means that they have to pay for all the work being done. In Canada the method of campaign and division of work is as follows: Officials of the federal department of entomology made a survey last year, and are continuing their survey at the present time. They had all possible information before them as to where outbreaks might be expected, so that municipalities and farmers affected would be equipped to meet it. Entomological officials of the federal department, officials of the experimental farms, and officials of our seed branch, together with officials of the provincial governments met and set up a central committee which undertook an educational campaign throughout the west. Upwards of 1,400 committees were established to take care of the divisions into which the provinces had been divided. The provinces were to supply poison and bait. In that connection they ran into some difficulty because the price of bran rose quickly through the demand for that commodity. It was used in a fifty-fifty ratio with sawdust and with water and poison and was to be broadcast as thinly as possible as bait. As a result of the rise in the price our officials in western Canada

undertook a study of some substitute for bran. A substitute was found which was almost as good and whether or not the fact it was found had any direct bearing on the drop in the price of bran I should not like to say definitely, although we feel it had. The fact is that bran dropped considerably in price. That bait has been purchased and distributed, ready for operation in the campaign. The municipalities take the responsibility for the distribution of this bait and the farmers themselves do the work of applying the poisoned bait in their own time. They are responsible on, their own farms. It is believed by those in the best position to judge that this method, with the expenditure we have made, is the most effective method that could be employed, because it puts the responsibility directly on the farmer but involves no cash outlay on his part. If they carry out this plan the way we believe they will, we think it possible to save from the prospective crop fourteen out of the fifteen bushels from the grasshopper menace. We have an example in the vicinity of Lake Carlyle, in Saskatchewan,, where individual farmers who applied this bait, which has to be applied in sunlight, at temperatures varying from 65 to 85 degrees did save their crop almost entirely. They estimated a loss of about one bushel per acre, while farmers adjoining who did not do this work lost practically their whole crop. But we have every hope this year, with the cooperation between the American officials and our own, that it will- be possible absolutely to control the grasshopper menace so long as there is no letting up of activity. But to show the danger we run into in certain parts of the west because of people giving out information that the menace was not as bad as our officials had reported, this year the officials in a certain municipality went out to a certain area where we had reported a severe outbreak as likely, and took the machine with which the soil is shaken to count the eggs, and after a good deal of work on their part reported that the danger had oeen very much overestimated. Our officials vent there to check up, and taking these people with them, showed them, by the proper method of finding out how many eggs there were, that from fifty to one hundred eggs were present per square foot and that we had been very conservative in our estimate. The trouble was that the officials of the municipality who had gone out were so vigorous in making the test that they not only shook out the earth but the eggs as well. Our committees are very wide awake to see that there 
will be no lessening of their energy and no lessening of their appreciation of the difficulty that is in front of them. This bait and the poison had to be bought, and so far as I am aware, and I have been more closely in contact with the situation, than anyone else in the government, every request so far as finances are concerned has been fully met, so that the poisoned bait and everything that goes with it can be purchased.

I have no fault
to find with that at all. We all know that they started good and early and distributed the poison betimes. But what I pointed out last Friday was also true. It was on the last lap of the hopper fight that the campaign fell down last year, for want of poison, and I drew the attention of the government to the fact that the estimates for entomology were reduced to one-half of what they were in 1931 and that no special grant was in sight in Canada as there was in the United States, where $2,000,000 had been appropriated. I pointed out that we were in danger again of a vastly greater territory being infected this year with grasshopper eggs, and that if we were to run short again of grasshopper poison during the last lap of the campaign the insects would take their flight, and of course, scatter all over the rest of the province.
I have nothing but commendation to give to the minister for starting earlier in the campaign, but what I wanted to know was, where was the money to correspond with the United States grant? The Brime Minister justified the small vote this year on the ground that it would not be needed, that the grasshoppers were receding, and that less money would be required, showing that he did not know the first thing about it. I pointed out that that was a longJbow stretcher of a statement to begin with. I pointed out that they were not receding, that it was the worst and most terrific invasion of grasshoppers that we have ever seen and that more money was required. The Prime Minister went on for 'half an hour or more, answering either myself or the hon. member for South IBattleford (Mr. Vallance) or the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and pointing out that the money voted, while it was less, was being efficiently administered; that the grasshoppers were disappearing and that we did not need so much money. Then someone must have given him a tip, because he began to say something about something being given, after I had suggested drawing on the vote for

peace, order and good government. I suggested, why could we not keep peace and order with the grasshoppers as well as with anything else, but there was no response even to that. Then after a little while the Prime Minister wakened up to the fact that there really were more grasshoppers there than last year and he said they had arranged to make a loan for that purpose to the west. May I ask the minister when the recommendation went to council on which the order in council was based? Of course, a recommendation is always sent to council by some minister before an order in council is passed. Was that recommendation sent by the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Labour? The Prime Minister said last Friday that the Minister of Agriculture always attended to such requirements, and naturally ,1 would suppose he would look after it. When was that recommendation sent to council, and by whom? Does the minister know what day the order in council was passed?

The understanding was this. We received various requests because we are very closely in touch with the committee of the provincial governments with a view to making this campaign thoroughly effective. We have been in touch with them from time to time and have assured them that whatever was necessary to carry out this campaign would ibe given, as it has been in the past in connection with various relief works and other works. They received this money from the banks, the banks having been given the assurance that when the required amount was purchased-and no one could say exactly what that amount was-the money would be forthcoming.
So far as the information last week is concerned, I myself received a telegram from western Canada before the discussion took place in the house at all.
Dealing with another point while I am on my feet, the hon. member asks why this vote is cut in two. He will remember, I am sure, the way it was done when he was Minister of Agriculture. This used to be under a vote for the Destructive Insect and Pest Act and the money divided between the experimental farms branch and the entomological branch, but this year it was felt more advisable, in order that the officials in charge could make their plans ahead, to divide the vote, giving the experimental farm their part and the entomological branch theirs, which is the item under discussion. Not only that, but actually there is a slight increase this year as compared
with last in what was given to the entomological branch. So, instead of a decrease in the vote there has been a slight increase.

I think I knew most of that except that I did not know the half, 8350,000 was more than the whole, $700,000, and I do not know that yet. My hon. friend forgot to tell me when the recommendation went to council.
I could not say exactly. I believe it is the finance minister who submits the recommendation in such cases as this.

There was a meeting of council, apparently. I do. not want to ask my hon. friend what occurred in council, but somebody must have sent a recommendation upon which the order in council was based. I anticipate that it would be the Minister of Finance in the event of a loan being required and made. That would be in his department. But either he or somebody else must have made a recommendation to council. It seems to me we cannot get this information. They do not want us to get close to the matter. There should be a record of the recommendation to council. Every order in council is based on somebody's recommendation, and it should not be a difficult matter to produce it. I do not think, Mr. Chairman, I should be accused of being oversuspicious in the absence of something being given to the committee beyond a nice dissertation on what was done last fall, all of which we knew. I asked a question as to when the recommendation was made to council, when it was signed, who signed it and when the order itself was signed.

I do not think the hon. member has got the point. An understanding was reached with the government of Saskatchewan that they were to proceed to make every possible preparation to meet this grasshopper menace, and this was made months ago.
That is quite all right.

We have been in almost continuous contact with them. As I stated, a telegram came from Regina stating what had been purchased, what their indebtedness was for it and asking that money be sent.
_ Mr. MOTHERWELL: I know that. I think all this money is spent in advance; a loan is obtained from the bank and then
